Reading Combate by machine

A workers' newspaper of the Portuguese revolution, read by computer: its drawings found and catalogued, its columns turned into text.

51 issues, 487 pages, 1974 to 1978. Every page can be read here, and every drawing the project has catalogued can be opened at full resolution.

Browse the issues How the reading is done

In this paper, the drawings carry the argument

In most newspapers an illustration decorates an article. In Combate it often is the article. A two-panel cartoon does the work of an editorial; a photographed wall poster reports a strike; a page of somebody's handwriting is printed whole because it came from the factory floor.

A text-first pipeline treats all of that as noise and throws it away. This project does the opposite. Every drawing, photograph, engraving, masthead and handwritten facsimile is located on its page, given a type and a description, and tied to the issue it came from.

The scans make this harder than it sounds. They are grey and low in contrast, unevenly lit, with ink bleeding through from the back of the sheet, and the layout follows no template from one page to the next. Off-the-shelf tools fail on them without preparation.

That difficulty is also what makes the corpus useful. It is a hard, real test case for machine reading under bad conditions, and it is open: the scans, the code and the catalogue are all in one public repository.

Method

Five stages, from the scanned PDF to a catalogue

The project reads Combate with classical computer vision and open-source OCR, no trained neural networks. Everything below was developed on the newspaper's own pages, one stage at a time, and each stage ships with the code that runs it. The first three stages are automatic; the last two are automatic first and checked by hand afterwards.

  1. 1 Acquisition51 PDFs from the library scans
  2. 2 RasterisationEach page becomes a bitmap
  3. 3 Layout segmentationText zones and graphic zones
  4. 4 Text recognitionPrinted columns through OCR
  5. 5 CataloguingRegions verified and described
1Acquisition

Collecting the newspaper

The 51 issues were gathered as PDF files, one per issue: 487 pages in all, between 2.2 and 8.1 MB each. The paper originals are held by the Biblioteca Nacional de Portugal; the digital copies used here were scanned from that collection and circulated through the Marxists Internet Archive, whose source line still runs across the top of every page.

The scans are the raw material for everything that follows, and they set the terms. They are greyscale, about 150 pixels per inch in most issues, with a dark ragged band where the sheet met the scanner glass. Nothing was retouched before processing: the pipeline has to cope with the pages as they are, because that is the condition of most digitised newspapers.

2Rasterisation

Turning each page into a bitmap

A PDF page is not an image. It is a list of instructions: place this stream of pixels here, draw this line there. Computer vision and OCR libraries cannot read instructions; they read grids of numbers. So the first thing the pipeline does is render every page into a bitmap, a rectangular grid in which each cell, a pixel, holds one grey value from 0 (black ink) to 255 (white paper).

The rendering is done with pypdfium2, the Python binding of Chrome's PDF engine. Each page is drawn at 150 dots per inch, in greyscale, with anti-aliasing on, and handed to OpenCV as an array. Page 3 of issue 1, for example, measures 1117 × 1582 points in the PDF and becomes an array of 3296 rows and 2328 columns: 7.7 million numbers.

Why 150 dpi and not more? The scans themselves were made at roughly that resolution, so rendering higher adds pixels without adding detail, and 487 pages at 300 dpi would take four times the memory and time for no gain. At 150 dpi the thinnest cartoon outlines are still two or three pixels wide, which is enough for the next stage to follow them.

The other thing this stage fixes is the coordinate system. Every box the project records is written as fractions of the page, from 0 to 1, measured from the top-left corner, never in pixels. A region found on a 150 dpi bitmap can therefore be cut again from a 300 dpi render, or drawn by this website on a page the browser has rendered at whatever size fits the screen. That one convention is what lets the catalogue, the detector and the viewer share the same data.

3Layout segmentation

      

        
Separating the text from the drawings

        
Combate has no page grid. Columns change width from article to article, headlines are drawn by hand, and a cartoon can sit anywhere. Template matching, which works on professionally set newspapers, has nothing to match against here. So the segmentation does not look for a layout at all. It looks at the ink, and asks of every mark on the page one question: does this look like body text, or does it not?

        
The work is done in five moves, all with OpenCV:

        
Binarise. The grey bitmap becomes ink or paper, nothing in between. Because the exposure is uneven, each pixel is compared with the average of its own neighbourhood (a 51-pixel window) rather than with one threshold for the whole page. This keeps faint ink in the dark corners and drops the grey haze in the bright ones.

        
Remove rules and border. Column filets and frames are long straight lines; they are found by eroding the ink with very wide and very tall kernels, and subtracted. The dark band at the edge of the scan is removed the same way. Without this step, a single rule can glue a cartoon to the column beside it into one giant region.

        
Mask the text. Body type is made of small marks. Every connected blob of ink is measured, and any blob no taller than a line of type, and not too wide, is declared text. The thresholds are fractions of the page height, not pixel counts, so they scale with each scan. A hand-drawn headline fails the test, and is kept: it is graphic.

        
Group what is left. The remaining ink is dilated so that the strokes of one drawing touch, and each connected block becomes a candidate region. Blocks smaller than 0.4% of the page, or thinner than a column filet, are dropped. Blocks that touch, or nearly touch, are merged, so that a masthead's separate letters, or a drawing and its caption, become one region.

        
Classify. Each region gets a first label from its position, size and ink density: a wide band at the top of the page is a masthead; a dark, evenly filled block is a photograph; a short wide band is lettering; a very large block is a composed page; everything else is a drawing. These labels are a starting point for stage 5, not a verdict.


        

        
How this was worked out

        
The first version used one threshold for the whole page and a large dilation, and on nearly every page it returned a single region: the entire sheet. Two things caused that. The dark scan border touched everything, and the dilation joined text columns to the drawings between them. Removing the border and the rules fixed the first; the second needed a different idea of what text is.

        
An early text mask tried to find lines of type by joining glyphs horizontally. It worked on clean columns and failed wherever lines were tightly leaded or the scan was smudged, which in Combate is often. Measuring individual marks instead, and calling small marks text, turned out to be more robust, because it does not depend on lines being separable. The last change was to express every size threshold as a fraction of the page, since issue 25 is a landscape spread of 3744 pixels across while issue 20 is 1378; the same pixel count means different things on each.

4Text recognition

      

        
Reading the printed columns

        
Once the graphic regions are known, the printed text can be read without them getting in the way. The engine is Tesseract with its Portuguese model, called from Python through pytesseract. But Tesseract run directly on a raw scan of Combate produces little of use, so the page is prepared first, in four steps.

        
Deskew. The tilt of the ink is measured from the binarised page and the bitmap is rotated back to horizontal. A scan of a folded newspaper is rarely straight, and even one degree of tilt costs Tesseract whole words at the ends of lines.

        
Denoise and flatten. Scanner grain is removed with a non-local means filter. Then the local paper tone is estimated with a wide median blur and the page is divided by it, which evens out the exposure: grey ink on grey paper in one corner and black ink on white in another become the same thing everywhere.

        
Stretch the contrast. Adaptive histogram equalisation (CLAHE) sharpens the difference between ink and paper tile by tile, without blowing out the parts that were already clear.

        
Mask the graphics. Every region from stage 3 is painted white. This is why segmentation comes first: a caption lettered inside a cartoon, or the slogan on a placard, would otherwise be read as a stray line of the article next to it and land in the wrong paragraph.

        
The prepared page then goes through Tesseract in automatic page segmentation mode (--psm 3), which lets the engine find the columns on its own; there is no grid to hand it. The output is the text, and for every word a confidence score, which the project keeps so that weak passages can be found and checked later.


        

        

          
Handwriting is not OCR. Combate printed facsimiles of handwritten communiqués, letters and posters, and there are enough of them that ignoring them would distort the record. They are found by stage 3 and set aside here, because a printed-text engine returns nonsense on them. They are the subject of a separate handwritten text recognition (HTR) effort, which needs a model trained on the corpus itself.

5Cataloguing

      

        
Verifying and describing the graphics

        
Stage 3 finds candidates; it does not know what they mean. The catalogue is the layer where a person looks at each region against its page, keeps or corrects its box, gives it a type from a fixed list, and writes a title and a note saying what it shows. That is what the illustrations page of this site reads from.

        
The verification happens in the issue viewer on this site. Any page can be opened, Mark an illustration turned on, and a box dragged over a drawing; the box is stored in the same page-relative coordinates as the detector's output, and can be exported as JSON to be added to the catalogue file in the repository. One record per region:


{
  "issue": 20,                       // issue number, 1 to 51
  "page": 5,                         // page within the issue PDF
  "box": [0.05, 0.50, 0.36, 0.205],  // x, y, width, height, 0 to 1
  "type": "illustration",            // cartoon · photograph · engraving ·
                                     // handwriting · masthead · composed block
  "title": "So juntos venceremos",
  "note": "Masthead of the Massarelos residents' committee bulletin."
}

        
Nothing on this site stores an image of a region. Each one is cut live from the PDF, at the resolution the screen needs, using nothing but these six fields. If a box is corrected in the catalogue, every view of it changes at once.

      

    


    

      
Why it matters

      

        
Digitised newspapers are usually made searchable by running OCR and discarding whatever is not text. For a paper like Combate, that discards the argument: the cartoons, the reproduced leaflets, the handwritten pages that were printed precisely because they were handwritten. Treating graphic regions as primary sources, with coordinates and descriptions, puts that material back in reach of historians, and does it for a whole run rather than a few famous images.

        
The method is also deliberately plain. Adaptive thresholds, connected components and a public OCR engine can be understood, checked and re-run by anyone with a laptop, and every parameter that matters is a fraction of the page rather than a magic number. A trained model would probably score higher; it could not be inspected, and it could not be reproduced without its training set. For a small, badly scanned corpus, legibility of the method is worth more than the last few points of accuracy.

        
Limitations, stated plainly

        
There is no hand-labelled ground truth for this corpus, so no formal precision figure is quoted. Spot checks suggest that roughly one candidate region in five is a false alarm, most often a bold multi-line headline read as a drawing, or a dense smudged block of text read as a photograph. First labels from stage 3 are the weakest layer; on badly smudged pages, lettering and photographs are regularly confused. Boxes are generous rather than tight, because the merge step prefers to keep a caption with its drawing than to split them. OCR confidence is high on clean pages and low on smudged ones, and the two cannot always be told apart in advance.

        
Reproduce it

        
The three scripts above are the complete detector. With a clone of the repository:


pip install pypdfium2 opencv-python-headless numpy pytesseract
# Tesseract itself and its Portuguese model: apt install tesseract-ocr tesseract-ocr-por

python3 rasterise.py /path/to/repository pages/      # stage 2: 487 bitmaps + pages.json
python3 segment.py   pages/ regions.json             # stage 3: candidate regions
python3 ocr.py       pages/ regions.json text/       # stage 4: one .txt per page

        

      

    

  







  

    
About

    

      

        

          
The project

          
COMBAT — Computational OCR/ATR Methods for Combate: Comics, Images and Text — applies machine reading to a newspaper that resists it, and treats its graphic content as evidence rather than decoration. The scans, the code, the catalogue and this site live in one public repository.

          
Who made it

          
Developed and maintained by Pedro João Oliveira.

          
Licence

          
The code and the catalogue are released under the GNU General Public License v3.0. The newspaper scans remain subject to the rights of their holders and are reproduced for research and study.

        

      

      

        

          
The newspaper

          
Combate ran from June 1974, weeks after the Carnation Revolution, into 1978. It described itself as a paper of the workers themselves, and it looked like it: hand-lettered headings, drawings by contributors, reprinted leaflets and communiqués, and a layout that changed from page to page. Its line, printed under the masthead of the first issue, was that the emancipation of the workers is the work of the workers themselves.

          
Sources

          
Paper collection: Biblioteca Nacional de Portugal. Digital copies: Marxists Internet Archive. Because the scans are poor, anything used as evidence should be checked against the paper copy.
